blurb: The campaign begins with coffee and rising dread. The Remote is gone. The house is warming up.
The hallway: every item left by every family member who is not home. The correct jacket is under all of it.
Dad opened the door to the garage. He now deeply regrets opening the door to the garage.
The garage depths. The emergency release cord is seventeen feet away. It might as well be in another country.
The car is free. But the house must be secured first. This will take five minutes. It will not take five minutes.
Dad is upstairs. He came up here for something. The reason has been lost to the stairs.
The attic contains the answer to a question nobody remembers asking.
The master bedroom. Everything Dad needs is in this room. None of it is where it should be.
The car is out, the journey could begin. The neighbor has emerged.
It was never just a room. It was a final exam. The Garage has awakened.
The hardware store parking lot. There are no spots. There are never spots. Dad will find one.
The cart return zone. The carts are not where they should be. One has escaped.
The contractors have established dominion over the north lot. Their morning is going better than Dad's.
The entrance gauntlet: a seasonal display, a donation bin, a flyer man, and a former coworker.
The lumber aisle. Dad needs screws. The screws are near the lumber. The lumber is everywhere.
The fastener aisle. There are 847 types of screw. Dad needs one. The system requires a degree.
Appliance parts. The dryer needs a part. The aisle assumes Dad knows his model number.
The tool display. Dad has all the tools. Dad is now holding a drill that feels different from his drill.
Self-checkout. Dad has found the part. Now he must survive the purchase.
He appeared from nowhere. He knows where everything is. The Floor Manager will upsell Dad into a better version.
The park entrance. Parking is worse than the hardware store. The 5K is finishing. Dad is in the chute.
The cleats were left 'by the goalpost.' There are twelve goalposts.
The equipment shed: lost items, broken nets, a lost-and-found nobody has checked since March.
The dog show has taken over Field 5. Dad must cross it.
The farmers market. Dad does not need anything here. He will spend forty-seven dollars.
The produce section. The tomatoes are the same tomatoes as the grocery store. They cost more. Dad buys six.
The craft vendor corridor. Dad has no interest in any of it. Dad is now holding a wind chime.
The food truck gauntlet. Dad is hungry. Two trucks have forty-minute waits. The rest he does not understand.
The birthday party for a child named Brayden or Cayden or possibly Hayden has escaped its zone.
She has been here since 5 AM. She has a radio, a floor plan, and opinions about Dad's parking.
Vastco. Dad cannot find his membership card. This is not a store you enter on goodwill.
The parking lot perimeter. No spots near the entrance. Dad will park far and walk. This is fine. Relatively.
The Vastco cart is not a cart. It is a commercial vehicle. It handles like a barge.
The sample corridor. Movement drops to thirty percent. The cheese is very good.
Paper goods. Enough paper towels to last until the kids graduate college. This is the rational choice.
The food section. The rotisserie chicken. Also the giant muffins. These were not on the list.
Electronics. Dad does not need electronics. Dad is now standing in front of a 75-inch television.
Clothing. Dad's fleece is fine. Dad now has two new fleeces.
The checkout line. Six lanes, fourteen carts each. Self-checkout is fifteen items. Dad has thirty-one.
She controls the desk, the returns, and the renewals. The Membership Desk Guardian controls Dad.
The soccer complex. Twenty-four fields. The bracket is in font size 8. The QR code is in the group chat.
Dad was told his son is on Field 7B. Fields 1 through 6 are visible. Field 7 is conceptual.
The snack stand is a beacon. The prices are audacious. Dad buys everything.
The team is here. Dad's son needs his shin guards. The shin guards are in the car. The car is now far away.
The sideline claim. The good spots are taken. The good-spot parents have been here since 10 AM.
Dad has opinions. Dad is expressing opinions. The coach can hear Dad.
Halftime is eight minutes. Dad must secure orange slices, water, and which quarter it actually is.
The sports dad convention. Their own civilization, their own language, their own opinions about refs.
The referee has made a call. The referee was correct. Dad does not know this.
She has been here since 6 AM. She controls the bracket, the fields, and Dad's afternoon.
Jefferson Middle School. On a Saturday. The school is not supposed to be open. The school is open.
The main hallway. The lockers are the same. Something is fundamentally different and Dad cannot name it.
The gymnasium: a team meeting, a cheer practice, a robotics demo, and a fog machine that should not be here.
The locker room corridor. Dad is not supposed to be here. Dad is here. It smells like 1987.
The east wing. Dad took a wrong turn. There are signs for the PTA meeting. He does not process this in time.
The PTA meeting. It is about the spring fundraiser. Dad is nodding. Dad is learning.
Dad is now helping plan the spring fundraiser. This was not the plan.
The principal has stopped by to thank everyone. The principal also has a few items for the agenda.
Dad's son is done. Dad must exit the PTA meeting. There is, however, one more thing.
She knows every parent's name, their kids' names, and what they said they'd do last year and didn't.
The family restaurant lot. Same physics as the hardware store. Different clientele. Same chaos.
The host stand has a list. The wait is forty-five minutes. The host says it could be sooner. The host is optimistic.
The lobby has three chairs and seventeen people. The TVs are playing sports. Not the right sport.
The buzzer activates at twenty-seven minutes. Ahead of schedule. Dad is suspicious.
The menu negotiation. Nine burgers. Dad's son cannot choose among nine burgers.
The order relay. Everyone is ready except the person who just decided to change their order.
Food arrives in the wrong sequence. Half is here. Half is 'coming right out.'
The food is finished. Dad would like the check. The check has not arrived. The server is nowhere.
The check has arrived. Something on it is wrong.
Dad is trying to leave. The lobby is now standing-room-only. The Hostess controls all movement.
IDKEA. Nobody arrives on purpose. Everyone arrives eventually. The escalator takes carts. This is a warning.
The living room showroom. Dad is sitting on a sectional. The sectional is very comfortable.
The bedroom section. The pillows are four dollars each. Dad now has four pillows in the cart.
The kitchen section. Dad's kitchen could look like this. It would require replacing the entire kitchen.
The children's section. Dad's kids are grown. Dad is looking at a small tent.
The self-serve warehouse. The air is different here. Time moves differently. Row 14 is between Row 12 and Row 17.
Flat pack retrieval. The shelf weighs more than Dad expected. The cart steers worse than the Vastco barge.
The meatball cafe is mandatory. It is not technically mandatory. It is mandatory.
Checkout. The flat pack does not fit on the conveyor. Dad must hand-key the barcode. There are seven barcodes.
The shelf is home. The instructions are fourteen pages. Page 8 cannot be interpreted by existing technology.
Dad's car is back in the driveway. A citation notice is on the mailbox. It is about the length of the grass.
A child has built a lemonade stand in front of Dad's driveway. Dad has no cash. This requires diplomacy.
The HOA event has let out. Every attendee is driving through the neighborhood at once. None of them yield.
The neighbor across the street is waving. This is friendly. This will take twenty-five minutes.
The cul-de-sac. The center of the neighborhood universe. Dad circles it slowly, assessing.
The backyard. The sprinkler ran. Or it didn't. The Remote controls the sprinkler. Dad does not have the Remote.
Three violation notices in the neighborhood today. Dad has one. The solidarity discussion has begun.
Dad walks the dog. The dog walks Dad. The dog has an agenda.
Dad is preparing the final run to the Community Center. The neighbor has noticed he is going somewhere.
He is watering his already-perfect lawn at 8:20 PM on a Saturday, because he saw Dad's car in the driveway.
The Community Center lot. The meeting ended two hours ago. The HOA President does not leave when it ends.
The lobby: a bulletin board, the by-laws laminated to fourteen pages, and a sign-in sheet.
The multipurpose room smells like coffee made at 6 PM. The screen still shows Slide 7 of Community Values.
The kitchen was cleaned with the thoroughness of someone who cleans when frustrated. They are still here.
The records hallway. A portrait of the President hangs here. The HOA budget paid for it.
The records room: every violation and grudge since 1987, organized with frightening precision.
The board room is empty. The Remote is not here. The agenda is partially erased.
The President has a private office. A nameplate, a file cabinet, a small refrigerator with a labeled lunch.
Full circle. The lobby. Karen Blackwell is here. The Remote is clipped to her clipboard.
Karen Blackwell. President since 2019. Unopposed. She has the Remote, the citation, and a binder.
